Fermat Point

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: This is a drawing, not a game: it shows the spot where the walk from all three corners of a triangle is shortest.
How to play: Drag the blue points, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, the hint or the Fermat point, then press Reset diagram to start again.
Look for the math

Fermat asked where to stand so that the walk to three given places is as short as possible. The picture turns each side of the triangle into an equilateral triangle, and the answer appears where three long lines cross.

A broken line made straight

Pick any point P inside the triangle ABC. Turn the segment BP by 60° about B; P goes to P' and A goes to C'. The little triangle BPP' is equilateral, so PB = P'P, and the turn keeps lengths, so PA = C'P'. Therefore PA + PB + PC = C'P' + P'P + PC, a broken line from C' to C. A straight line is the shortest path between two places, so the sum is smallest exactly when P lies on CC'. The same argument from the other two corners puts P on AA' and BB' too. Those lines are the ones drawn here, and they meet at the Fermat point F.

Three new corners

A', B' and C' are the far corners of the three outward equilateral triangles on the sides — the configuration of Napoleon's theorem. At F the three lines cross at 120°, and the three angles around F are all 120°. The linked page also claims AA' = BB' = CC' = FA + FB + FC. The logic test confirms all of these on hundreds of non-obtuse triangles, to within a millionth: it checks the angles, the crossings, the equal lengths and the minimum itself by independent numerical search.

When a corner is too wide

The construction fails when an angle of ABC is 120° or more; then that corner is the answer. The test checks hundreds of such triangles: the corner wins the minimum, and the sum of the three unit directions from it has length at most 1, which is the mathematical way to say that moving away cannot help. The status line names the winning corner whenever this happens, just as the applet's 120° test does.

The fourth point and the hint

The green point D starts at the centroid (A + B + C) / 3 but can be dragged independently, as in the applet. The hint draws three groups of equal lengths, such as AD = ADb = CpDc, and three 60° arcs at D; the test verifies those equalities on every generated triangle. When D is dragged to within one pixel of F the original applet brightens the three long lines; here they are drawn faintly all the time and brightened in that same case. The status line then calls D "F", again matching the applet's one-pixel rule.

Try dragging a corner until one angle passes 120°: the meeting point jumps to that corner.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
